newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Violence up in Haiti, U.N. wants its troops to stay.
newsitem.headline: Violence up in Haiti, U.N. wants its troops to stay.

text.p: With violence on the rise in Haiti, particularly from ex-soldiers loyal to the deposed dictatorship, the United Nations said on Thursday it could not reduce its military and civilian personnel.
The U.N. Security Council in July, at the insistence of China, had requested the United Nations consider further reductions in Haiti personnel this month.

But Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, in a report, said that the present troop level, already whittled down by China, constitutes "the minimum required for implementation of the mission's mandate."

He blamed most of the violence on rightwing groups, some loyal to the former military junta, although he said police had also abused their authority. With unemployment high and funds scarce, he said the government had few means to train and equip police and the judicial force properly.
The United Nations has over 1,200 troops, half of them funded by Canada and the United States. It also has 270 civilian police with the United States sending another 25 shortly.
Their mandate expires at the end of November and Washington and Ottawa are expected to seek another extension.
In his report, Boutros-Ghali said it was clear that "the security situation in Haiti has deteriorated in recent weeks."

Neither the newly-formed civilian police force nor President Rene Laval's security detail, whose chief and deputy were suspended for suspected crimes, are yet able to cope with rightists and criminals challenging them.
With funds scarce and foreign contributions low, police officers are paid two months late, were underequipped and often wear civilian clothes because of lack of uniforms.
The judicial system is still in shambles before and after the military junta was deposed, causing many to seek "vigilante justice," the report said.

"The attacks and shooting incidents that have occurred in Port-au-Prince reflect an increase in subversive activities in which some ex-(soldiers) and members of extreme rightist organisations seem to be involved," the report said.

Former President Jean-Bertrande Aristide, overthrown in a miitary coup in 1991 and put back into office by the United States in 1994, had disbanded the military. But its officers and soldiers were systematically disarmed and are demanding back pay and pensions.
The report said they were the prime suspects of vigilante incidents in August and plots against the government as well as threats against U.N. and American personnel.

Although these groups lack the capacity to pose a serious threat to the government, the "pattern of incidents has caused disquiet among Haitians and dealt another blow to the morale of the Haitian National Police," the report said.
